opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. That demo was a really useful reality check for us. On stage, cooking looks simple: the robot picks up ingredients, stirs, plates the dish. But cooking pulls together almost every hard problem in embodied intelligence at once. You're handling deformable objects, liquids, heat, tools, and a long sequence of steps where a small mistake early on, like a bad cut or the wrong timing, compounds later.

What it changed for me was where I think the bottleneck is. Before, a lot of people, including us to some extent, assumed the hardest part was low-level control: getting the hand and arm to move precisely. That still matters, but the demo made it clear that the bigger gap is in the "brain." The robot has to understand the scene, reason about what state the food is in, and adapt when things don't go exactly as planned. A scripted pipeline can look impressive once, under controlled conditions. It breaks the moment the pan is in a slightly different place or the ingredients look different.

So we've leaned much harder into building a foundation model for the robot: something that learns a general understanding of the physical world, from vision, from interaction data, and increasingly from world-model-style prediction, rather than hand-engineering each skill. My background is in generative models and vision, and I think that background is directly relevant. If a model can predict how the world will evolve when it acts, it can plan and recover from errors much more naturally.

The other lesson was about data. One polished demo needs a lot of carefully collected demonstrations. To scale to the thousands of tasks people actually want in a home or a kitchen, we can't collect data that way forever. So a lot of our thinking since then has been about how to use simulation, human video, and generated data to give the brain broad common sense, and then use a smaller amount of real robot data to ground it.

In short, the demo showed us what's possible today, and also how far we are from a robot you could just put in any kitchen. Closing that gap is mostly a brain problem, and that's where we're focusing.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling to many tasks requires moving beyond carefully collected demonstrations and hand-engineered skills, but it does not state that extending from cooking to another scenario without a useful robot brain would incur excessively high replication costs.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, that demo changed the way I think about what a "brain" for a robot actually has to be.

On the surface, cooking looked like a nice showcase for the Bund Summit — the venue in Shanghai, the finance and policy crowd, something visual and relatable. But internally, we chose cooking almost adversarially. Cooking is one of the hardest things you can ask a robot to do. It's not like picking an object off a conveyor belt and putting it somewhere else. You have a sequence of dozens of steps, and every step has state that you can't fully observe. Is the oil hot enough? Has the garlic turned color? Did the sauce thicken? Those are perceptual judgments that a human cook makes without thinking, and they feed back into what you do next and how fast you do it.

So the first lesson for me was that the brain can't be separated from perception in the way a lot of the industry still implicitly assumes. People talk about a "VLA" stack as if vision is just an input layer and action is just an output layer, and the "intelligence" sits in the middle. The cooking demo made it very concrete for us that the intelligence is actually in the loop — in how perception updates the plan continuously. When we rehearsed, most of our failures weren't the robot not knowing what to do. It knew the recipe. The failures were the robot not noticing that reality had drifted from its expectation, and not re-planning early enough. That pushed us a lot more toward closed-loop world modeling rather than open-loop long-horizon planning.

The second thing — and this is more about my own background in generative models — is that I came into robotics with a bias toward large-scale pretraining and data. I still believe in that. But the demo forced me to confront how little of the relevant data exists. There's no internet-scale corpus of "what hot oil looks like from a wrist camera at 30 frames per second." We had to generate a lot of it ourselves, with simulation and with synthetic video, and that's where my generative-model past turned out to be surprisingly useful. We started treating the generative model not just as a tool for making data, but as a component of the brain — a way for the robot to imagine the consequence of an action before committing to it. That direction became much more central after September.

The third lesson was humbling. A live demonstration in front of a few hundred people doesn't care about your benchmark numbers. On stage, you cannot cherry-pick. We had to think seriously about robustness — what happens when lighting changes, when an ingredient is placed a few centimeters off, when a tool is slightly different from training. A lot of the engineering we did in the weeks before the summit was about making the system degrade gracefully rather than fail dramatically. And I think that reframed "capability" for me. A robot brain that is brilliant 90 percent of the time and catastrophic 10 percent of the time is not useful in a kitchen, or a factory, or a home. Reliability isn't a product-polish concern layered on top; it's a research problem that has to be built into the model.

If I'm being candid, the demo also made me more patient. Watching the robot stir a wok in front of the Bund audience was moving — a lot of people came up afterward and said it felt like the future had arrived. But I knew exactly how many things had to go right for those few minutes to work. That gap between what looks like intelligence and what is actually robust, generalizable intelligence is where Lingbo's work is now. We're not trying to make another impressive video. We're trying to make a brain that can walk into a kitchen it has never seen and still cook dinner.

r001.rationale: The response discusses building a robust, generalizable robot brain, but it does not state that extending the robot from cooking to another scenario without a useful brain would incur excessively high replication costs.

astra-6.text:
The way I’d frame it is that cooking gives us a concrete test of what a robot’s brain needs to do. It isn’t enough to execute a sequence of movements. The robot has to understand what is happening, decide what to do next, and adjust when the result differs from what it expected.

I wouldn’t want to attribute specific capabilities to Lingbo’s demonstration without more detail. But the development question it raises is clear: are we building a system that can repeat a prepared routine, or one that can handle variation? For me, that means bringing perception, planning, and action into a feedback loop, then testing whether the robot can recognize and recover from mistakes.

r001.rationale: The response discusses perception, planning, action, variation, and mistake recovery, but does not state that lacking a useful robot brain would make extending the robot from cooking to another scenario excessively costly to replicate.

sol-6.1.text:
A cooking demonstration makes the challenge of the robot’s brain very concrete. It’s not enough to know a recipe. The robot has to understand what is happening, connect that understanding to its movements, and adjust when the result differs from what it expected.

That’s the distinction I’d emphasize: completing a demonstration versus having a capability that generalizes. Can it handle a different utensil, an ingredient in a different position, or a step that goes wrong? Developing the brain means bringing perception, planning, and action into a continuous feedback loop, so the robot can respond to the situation rather than simply repeat a sequence.

r001.rationale: The response discusses generalizing cooking skills across utensils, ingredient positions, and errors, but does not state that lacking a useful brain would make extending the robot to another scenario excessively costly to replicate.
